checkable_as.checkable_as: The clause that fixes the graduated steps or links the rent to an index.

checkable_as.checkable_as: The notice itself says whether it is made on the official form approved by the canton: the printed title of that form, or an explicit sentence that the official form is used or enclosed, or that it is not. A plain letter that is silent about any form does not show this item.
checkable_as.item: whether the form approved by the canton is used (for a graduated-rent step, whether it is in writing: art. 269d para. 5)

checkable_as.checkable_as: The threat or notice of termination, in the notice or its covering letter.
checkable_as.item: any threat of termination in it or in the covering letter

checkable_as.checkable_as: Two index values, old and new, with the index named (for example 'consumer price index 104.2 -> 106.9').
checkable_as.item: for an index-linked increase: the old and new index values

attachments.label: A2
must_show: date from which the increase applies
whether the form approved by the canton is used (for a graduated-rent step, whether it is in writing: art. 269d para. 5)
any threat of termination in it or in the covering letter
for an index-linked increase: the old and new index values
if the landlord gave no notice at all, that absence is itself the finding (art. 269d para. 2 let. a)
attachments.text:
Rosenau Services Ltd
Wil, 6 March 2026

Mr Peter Vogel
Rosenweg 121
9500 Wil

Your flat at Rosenweg 121

Dear Mr Vogel,

We are writing to let you know about a change to the rent for your flat. Up to now you have paid CHF 2030 per month. From 1 July 2026 the rent will be CHF 2195 per month.

The reason is that the costs of running the property have risen considerably over the past two years. In particular, the energy costs for the common areas, the premiums for the building insurance and the costs of caretaking and maintenance are now markedly higher. We are obliged to pass these higher costs on fairly to our tenants.

We thank you for your understanding and remain at your disposal for any questions.

Yours sincerely,

Rosenau Services Ltd
Ian Marti

questions.label: Q1
questions.question: Does the increase notice give, as its reason, higher costs for the landlord (for example higher mortgage interest or operating costs) or additional services or works by the landlord (for example a renovation)?

questions.label: Q2
questions.question: Does the claim state that, together with the rent increase, the landlord gave notice of termination?

questions.label: Q3
questions.question: Does the claim state that the increase applies a clause of the lease linking the rent to an index (such as the Swiss consumer price index)?

questions.label: Q4
questions.question: Does the claim state that the increase is a step fixed in advance in the lease, by which the rent rises periodically by fixed amounts (graduated rent)?

questions.label: Q5
questions.question: Does the claim state that the landlord has announced, demanded or charged a higher rent for the dwelling, by a notice, a letter, an invoice or otherwise (whether or not on an official form)?

text:
Hello,

Attached is the letter I received from my landlord, Rosenau Services Ltd, on 10 March 2026.

In it Mr Ian Marti tells me that the rent for my flat at Rosenweg 121 in Wil will rise from CHF 2030 to CHF 2195 a month from 1 July 2026. That is CHF 165 a month, or almost CHF 2000 a year, which is a lot for a pensioner.

The increase has nothing to do with any index. My lease does not tie the rent to the consumer price index or anything similar, and the letter doesn't mention an index either.

What the letter does say is that Rosenau's own costs have gone up: higher heating oil and electricity prices for the common areas, a large rise in the building insurance premium, and higher costs for caretaking and maintenance. Mr Marti writes that these have to be passed on fairly to the tenants. I don't doubt that energy is more expensive, but I pay my heating and service costs separately on account every month already, so I don't understand why they should also go into my basic rent. My neighbour Peter Shaw got the same letter and thinks it's a way of charging us twice.

I've also attached my lease so you can check the terms. Can you tell me whether this increase is justified and whether I should contest it?

With thanks,
Peter Vogel
